name: The Last Day of School
blurb: A time capsule from five years ago, and the things six people never said out loud
title: The Last Day of School: Drama Skit Script for 6 People
description: A 6-minute heartfelt drama skit with laughs for 6: on the last day of school, a time capsule brings out the things nobody ever said. Free to perform.
h1: The Last Day of School: a 6-Minute Drama Skit Script for 6 People
logline: On the final afternoon of school, a teacher brings out a time capsule the class filled when they were eleven. The first letters are funny. Then each one asks a question someone has been avoiding for five years, and the last day becomes the day they finally say it.
setting: A classroom being packed up at the end of the year. Props: a shoebox wrapped in tape, envelopes with letters, a child's drawing, a friendship bracelet, a few sheets of paper, a folded paper star.

roles.name: Ms. Rowe
roles.note: Adult teacher, any gender (change the title to fit). Warm, a little dramatic, about to retire.

roles.name: Jade
roles.note: Teen, any gender. Funny, still scared of the dark, the first to hug.

roles.name: Tom
roles.note: Teen, written as a boy (any gender works). The joker, carrying a five-year-old apology.

roles.name: Hana
roles.note: Teen, any gender. Bright and loved, hiding the news of a move abroad.

roles.name: Eli
roles.note: Teen, any gender. Quiet, once very lonely, now quietly sure of their friends.

roles.name: Noor
roles.note: Teen, any gender. Kind and private. The secret author of a hundred paper stars.

script.scene: SCENE 1 – An almost empty classroom, the last afternoon of the school year

script.action: Chairs are stacked. Posters are half taken down. JADE, TOM, HANA, ELI and NOOR sit on desks. MS. ROWE enters carrying a dusty shoebox wrapped in tape.

script.say: Found it. Exactly where we buried it. At the back of the store cupboard, behind the paint.
We didn't bury it. We put it on a shelf.
It was a very dramatic shelf. Five years ago you were eleven, and you wrote letters to the people you'd be today. Shall we?

script.action: Everyone gathers. Ms. Rowe opens the box. Inside: envelopes, a drawing, a friendship bracelet.

script.say: Oh no. I remember writing mine. I was so serious.
Then you go first.

script.action: Tom opens an envelope and reads aloud.

script.say: "Dear future Tom. I hope you are famous. I hope you have a car. I hope you are a professional footballer AND a scientist." Then there's a drawing of me with muscles.

script.action: He holds up the drawing. Everyone laughs.

script.say: Are you famous?
I'm famous in my house. For leaving the fridge open.
My turn. "Dear Jade. Are you still scared of the dark? Have you learned to whistle? Please say yes."
Have you?

script.action: Jade tries to whistle. Only air comes out.

script.say: The dark, yes. Whistling, never.
Eli?

script.action: Eli opens a letter, reads silently first, then aloud, more quietly.

script.say: "Dear Eli. I hope by now you have one friend. Just one is fine."

script.action: The laughing stops.

script.say: I forgot I wrote that. I didn't talk to anyone for most of our first year.
I know.
You know?
There's something I never said. First week. Those boys threw your bag in the bin, and everyone laughed. I laughed. I didn't even think it was funny. I just didn't want to be next.

script.action: Silence. Tom looks at the floor.

script.say: I'm sorry. I've been sorry for five years. I just never found the right day to say it.

script.action: Eli looks at Tom for a long moment.

script.say: You took my bag out of the bin. After everyone left. I saw you. I thought you were stealing it.
I put it on your desk.
I know. That's how I knew there was one person here who wasn't so bad.

script.action: Tom laughs, a little wet-eyed. Eli puts out a fist. Tom bumps it.

script.say: So, one friend. Letter answered.
My go. Before I lose my nerve.

script.action: Noor opens a small envelope. A folded paper star falls out.

script.say: "Dear Noor. Did you ever tell them?"
Tell us what?

script.action: Noor takes a breath, then holds up the paper star.

script.say: Every time someone in this class had a bad day, they found one of these in their locker. Folded paper star. Nice note inside.
The star person! I got one when I failed my swimming test!
I got one after my grandad's funeral. I've still got it.
We all thought it was Ms. Rowe.
I thought it was the caretaker.
It was me. Five years. A hundred and twelve stars. I just liked knowing someone felt better and didn't have to say thank you.

script.action: Jade walks over and hugs Noor tightly.

script.say: Thank you.
That's the one thing I said you didn't have to say.
I'm saying it anyway.

script.action: Everyone turns to Hana, who is holding her letter but not opening it.

script.say: Hana?
I know what mine says. It says "I hope we are all still together forever."
Well, we are. Mostly.
We're not. I'm moving. My family's moving to another country in two weeks. I was going to tell you today. Then I was going to tell you at the end of today. And now it's the end of today.

script.action: Nobody speaks. The happiness drains out of the room.

script.say: Two weeks?
I'm sorry. Every time I tried, someone was laughing, and I didn't want to be the one who made it sad.

script.action: Noor folds a paper star from a corner of her letter and hands it to Hana.

script.say: Bad day. You get a star.

script.action: Hana laughs and cries at the same time.

script.say: Then we write new letters. Right now. To us in ten years. And Hana, you're coming back to open them.
From the other side of the world?
From the moon if you have to.
Paper's on my desk. Ten years. Be honest this time.

script.action: They each take a sheet and write. Ms. Rowe takes one last envelope from the bottom of the box.

script.say: Miss. That one's yours.
I didn't think you'd noticed.
Read it.
"Dear me. It's your last year before you stop teaching. If this class has turned out half as kind as they are at eleven, you did fine."

script.action: She folds the letter. Looks at them all.

script.say: More than half.

script.action: The students fold their new letters and drop them into the box one by one. Ms. Rowe closes the lid.

script.sfx: The final school bell rings, long and loud.

script.action: Nobody moves.

script.say: Can we stay five more minutes?
Five more minutes.

script.action: They sit close together on the desks around the box. Lights fade slowly.

ul: Stack a few chairs at the back and leave half-removed posters on the walls to show the room is being packed up. The students sit on desks in a loose half circle facing the audience.
The box is placed centre on a desk and everyone gathers around it. Each reader steps slightly forward to read, then returns to the group.
Make the paper star beforehand, plus one sheet Noor can fold or pretend to fold quickly for Hana.
During the new letters, keep the stage quiet and let everyone write for a few real seconds; it is the calm before Ms. Rowe's letter.

End on the image, not a line: after Five more minutes, the six sit close around the closed box and hold still as the lights fade. If you have no lights, someone says blackout softly or the group simply freezes for five seconds.
The game is the letters: each one is less funny and more true than the last. Tom's and Jade's get laughs, Eli's stops the laughing, Noor's and Hana's turn the room.
Eli's first letter is the turning point. Read it quietly, almost to yourself, and wait before the next line.
Tom's apology is not a speech. Short sentences, eyes on the floor, and a real struggle to say it.
Noor's reveal can get a laugh on A hundred and twelve stars. Let it, then let Jade's thank-you be completely sincere.
Hana must fight not to cry, not try to cry. Trying to be brave is what makes an audience feel it.
Common mistake: rushing after the bell. The long silence when nobody moves is the most important moment in the skit.
Set it at the end of a summer camp, a last day at a job, or the last rehearsal of a school club, with the capsule hidden on the first day.
For a cast of four or five, cut Jade and give the hug to Noor's thank-you moment, or combine Tom and Eli's story into one letter. For more, add letters with one funny line each.
Part-two hook: ten years later, the same six meet in the same room to open the new letters, and one chair stays empty until the very last line.

prompts.keyframe: Five teenagers and a teacher gathered around a dusty taped shoebox on a desk in a half-packed classroom, warm late afternoon sunlight through windows, stacked chairs behind, wide shot, cinematic still, 16:9
shots: Medium close-up, a quiet teenager reads a handwritten letter aloud as the smiles fade around them, warm golden light, slow push in, emotional mood
Close-up of hands folding a small paper star and passing it to a crying friend, shallow focus, soft afternoon light, tender mood
Wide static shot, a group of students sits close together on desks around a closed shoebox as a school bell rings and nobody moves, light slowly fades, bittersweet ending

faq.q: Is The Last Day of School suitable for a graduation or end-of-year assembly?
faq.a: Yes. It was written for exactly that: about six minutes, safe for all ages, funny at the start and moving at the end. It is free to perform and film under CC BY 4.0; credit "Script: cv.cm".

faq.q: Can we put our own memories into the letters?
faq.a: Please do. Keep the order: two light, funny letters first, then one that stops the laughing, then the biggest secret. Real details from your own class, like a school trip or a teacher's catchphrase, make it land harder.

faq.q: How do we rehearse the emotional moments without it feeling fake?
faq.a: Rehearse the sad lines flat at first, without trying to feel anything, until the timing is easy. Then play the pauses honestly. Characters who try to hide their feelings feel more real than characters who show them.
